title: Breach of Contract and its Remedies
outcomes: Distinguish actual breach from anticipatory breach and state the promisee's options under Section 39.
Compute damages under Section 73, applying the rule in Hadley v. Baxendale, the duty to mitigate and the kinds of damages.
Apply Section 74 to penalty and liquidated-damages clauses, including the Government-bond exception.
Explain the other remedies — rescission, quantum meruit, specific performance and injunction — and when each is available.

meta.exam_tip: Damages problems are frequent: compute the price difference neatly, then decide each head of special loss on the notice test (Hadley v. Baxendale). For any "penalty" clause, write "reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named — Section 74".

concepts.title: Breach of contract — meaning and kinds
body: Breach of contract means a party's failure to carry out his obligation under the contract, without lawful excuse.
It may be (1) actual — failure to perform on the due date, or during performance (e.g. stopping halfway); or (2) anticipatory — refusing, or disabling oneself from performing, before the due date.
Whatever the kind, the injured party is discharged from his own obligations and gets the remedies described in this unit.
concepts.analogy: Actual breach is not turning up for the match; anticipatory breach is announcing a week earlier that you will not come — or selling your kit to someone else.
concepts.work: When a customer cancels a confirmed order before the delivery date, a CA in industry recognises an anticipatory breach and advises on the claim and on the accounting for the cancelled order.

concepts.title: Anticipatory breach — Section 39
body: Section 39: if one party refuses to perform the whole of his promise, or puts himself in a position where he cannot perform it, the other party is entitled to terminate the contract — unless his own words or conduct show that he has agreed to let it continue.
It may be express (a clear statement: "I will not deliver") or implied by conduct (e.g. A agrees to sell his horse to B on 1 September, but sells it to C in August).

Effect: the promisee is excused from further performance and may choose either (1) to treat the contract as ended at once and sue for damages immediately, without waiting for the due date (Hochster v. De La Tour), or (2) to keep the contract alive and wait for the due date, then hold the other party liable. If he waits, he keeps the contract alive for both sides — the promisor may still perform, and if some later event (e.g. a change in law) excuses performance, the promisee may lose his claim (Frost v. Knight discussed the promisee's option to wait or sue at once).
concepts.analogy: If the caterer tells you in March he won't serve your May wedding, you can book another caterer and sue now — or hold him to it and wait, with the risk that comes with waiting.
concepts.work: Commodity buyers facing a supplier's cancellation often book a replacement at once — choosing option (1) — to limit price risk; the CA documents the date of acceptance of the repudiation, as damages are measured with reference to it.

concepts.title: Actual breach
body: Actual breach occurs when a party fails to perform on the due date (e.g. supplier does not deliver on 1 June), or during performance (e.g. a contractor abandons the building midway, or a singer engaged for twelve nights stays away from the sixth night).

The injured party may treat the contract as ended (Section 39 applies to refusal during performance too), is discharged from his own obligations, and may claim compensation. Where time was not of the essence (Section 55), he may instead allow extra time and claim compensation for the delay.
concepts.analogy: The bell has rung and the student has not written the paper — that is actual breach.
concepts.work: A CA preparing a claim for a client whose supplier failed to deliver gathers market rates on the due date — the starting point for damages.

concepts.title: Suit for damages — Section 73 and Hadley v. Baxendale
body: Section 73: the injured party may recover compensation for loss or damage (a) that arose naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or (b) that both parties, at the time of contracting, foresaw as a likely result of such a breach. No compensation is given for remote and indirect loss or damage.

Duty to mitigate: in assessing the loss, the court takes into account the means of remedying the inconvenience that were reasonably available — the injured party must take reasonable steps to reduce his loss and cannot recover loss he could have avoided.

Hadley v. Baxendale: a mill's broken crankshaft was handed to a carrier for delivery to the makers as a pattern. The carrier delayed. The mill-owner claimed loss of profits for the extra days the mill stood idle. Held: the loss of profit was not recoverable, because the carrier had not been told that the mill would be idle until the shaft returned — such loss was neither a natural consequence nor within the parties' contemplation.
Usual measure for goods: (market price on the due date − contract price) × quantity. Compensation is to make good the loss, not to punish.
concepts.analogy: Damages pay for the ripples you could foresee when you threw the stone, not for every wave that later reached a distant shore.
concepts.work: Claims for "consequential loss" (lost profits, penalties under other contracts) succeed only where the special circumstances were communicated at the time of contract — which is why CAs advise clients to state critical deadlines and end-uses in purchase orders.

concepts.title: Kinds of damages
body: Ordinary damages compensate for the natural, direct loss. Special damages require notice of the special circumstances at the time of contracting (if a carrier is told the mill is idle, it is liable for the mill's normal profit for the period of delay — but not for loss of an unusually profitable contract it was never told about).

Exemplary damages are awarded only in two cases: breach of promise to marry, and wrongful dishonour of a customer's cheque by a banker. A trader whose credit suffers may get substantial damages even without proof of money loss; a non-trader gets only nominal damages unless special loss is pleaded and proved (Gibbons v. Westminster Bank).

Nominal damages recognise a breach that caused no real loss. Where goods deteriorate because a carrier was late, damages are payable even though no notice was given. Pre-fixed damages are governed by Section 74 (next card).

blocks.title: Kinds of damages

concepts.analogy: Ordinary damages refill the glass you spilt; special damages also pay for the carpet — but only if you warned them about the carpet.
concepts.work: In claims against logistics providers, CAs separate ordinary loss (value of goods, deterioration) from special loss (production stoppage), because each needs different proof.

concepts.title: Penalty and liquidated damages — Section 74
body: Parties often name in the contract the sum payable on breach. English law distinguishes liquidated damages (a genuine pre-estimate of loss — recoverable in full) from a penalty (an extravagant sum fixed to frighten the other party into performing — not enforced beyond actual loss).

Indian law (Section 74) does not draw this distinction. Whether the sum is called a penalty or liquidated damages, the injured party gets reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named. The court will never award more than the named sum, but may award less.
Example: named sum ₹5,00,000. If the loss is ₹3,20,000, the award is ₹3,20,000; if the loss is ₹7,00,000, the award is limited to ₹5,00,000.

Guides to spotting a penalty: a sum far larger than any probable loss; an extra sum payable merely for delay in paying an amount (delay alone rarely causes such loss); a clause raising the interest rate once a default occurs can also be a penalty. The label used by the parties is not conclusive. A clause that the whole loan becomes due on default of one instalment is not a penalty.

Exception: where a person gives a bond or similar instrument to the Central or a State Government for performing a public duty or an act in which the public is interested, he is liable to pay the whole sum named on breach.
concepts.analogy: The named sum is a ceiling, not a price tag: the court fills the room with reasonable compensation up to, but never above, that ceiling.
concepts.work: Delay (LD) clauses in construction and IT contracts are routinely negotiated by CAs and finance teams; when deliveries slip, they estimate the provision on the basis of reasonable compensation capped at the clause amount.

concepts.title: Other remedies — rescission, quantum meruit, specific performance, injunction
body: Rescission: the injured party may treat the contract as rescinded; he is freed from his own obligations and, under Section 75, a person who rightfully rescinds is entitled to compensation for damage sustained through non-performance.

Quantum meruit ("as much as he has earned"): a claim for the value of work done or goods supplied. Conditions: the original contract must have been discharged (e.g. by the other party's breach), and the claim is made by the party not in default. It is restitutory (pays for value received), whereas damages are compensatory. Typical cases: an agreement discovered to be void or a contract that becomes void; work done not intended to be gratuitous; services rendered with no agreed fee; one party abandons or refuses to perform; a divisible contract partly performed and the benefit enjoyed; and a lump-sum contract fully but badly performed (lump sum payable, less a deduction for bad work).

Specific performance: where damages are not an adequate remedy (e.g. a contract for a unique painting or a particular piece of land), the court may, in its discretion, order the party in breach to perform the contract as agreed.

Injunction: where a party is doing something he promised not to do, the court may issue an order restraining him (e.g. an actor who agreed to act exclusively for one producer during a period may be restrained from acting for another producer during that period, though he cannot be forced to act for the first).
concepts.analogy: Damages pay for the broken promise; quantum meruit pays for the work already done; specific performance says "keep your promise"; an injunction says "stop breaking it".
concepts.work: When a client's contractor walks off a half-finished job, the CA helps value the work done (quantum meruit), the extra cost of completion (damages) and any liquidated damages (Section 74).

illustrations.title: Damages for non-delivery — market price rule
illustrations.q: Gopal agrees to supply 400 bags of sugar to Rekha at ₹2,800 a bag on 15 March. On 15 March the market price is ₹3,150 a bag and Gopal refuses to deliver. What damages can Rekha claim?

solution.provision: Section 73: compensation for loss arising naturally, in the usual course of things, from the breach. For non-delivery of goods, the natural loss is the excess of the market price on the due date over the contract price.
solution.facts: Contract price ₹2,800; market price on the due date ₹3,150; 400 bags not delivered.
solution.analysis: Rekha would have to pay ₹350 more per bag to buy the same sugar in the market.
solution.conclusion: Rekha can claim ordinary damages of ₹1,40,000.

checks.label: rise in price per bag on the due date
ordinary damages = quantity x (market price - contract price)

illustrations.title: Section 74 — named sum as a ceiling
illustrations.q: A software contract provides that the vendor will pay ₹5,00,000 as "liquidated damages" if the system is not live by 1 April. It goes live in July. Find the amount recoverable if the client's proved loss is (a) ₹3,20,000; (b) ₹7,00,000.

solution.provision: Section 74: if the contract fixes a sum to be paid on breach, the injured party is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named; Indian law does not distinguish between penalty and liquidated damages.
solution.analysis: In (a) reasonable compensation equals the loss, which is below the cap. In (b) the loss exceeds the cap, so the award stops at the named sum.
solution.conclusion: (a) ₹3,20,000; (b) ₹5,00,000 — the remaining ₹2,00,000 of loss cannot be recovered.

checks.label: case (a): reasonable compensation = loss proved, within the named sum
case (b): award capped at the sum named in the contract
case (b): loss that cannot be recovered beyond the cap

illustrations.title: Failure to mitigate
illustrations.q: Sana agrees to buy 250 units of packing material from Tushar at ₹1,200 each, delivery on 10 June. Tushar fails to deliver. On 10 June the material is freely available in the market at ₹1,340, but Sana waits two weeks and then buys at ₹1,460. She claims ₹65,000. How much can she recover?

solution.provision: Section 73: compensation for loss arising naturally from the breach; in estimating it, the means available for remedying the inconvenience must be taken into account — the injured party must take reasonable steps to mitigate the loss.
solution.facts: Contract price ₹1,200; market price on the due date ₹1,340; Sana delayed and paid ₹1,460.
solution.analysis: Sana could have bought at the market price on 10 June. The extra cost caused by her own delay is not a loss arising from the breach.
solution.conclusion: Sana can recover ₹35,000; ₹30,000 of her claim fails for want of mitigation.

checks.label: buyer's claim based on the price he actually paid
damages allowed: market price available on the due date
loss due to failure to mitigate — not recoverable

illustrations.title: Quantum meruit — instalment contract
illustrations.q: Ajay agrees to deliver 120 bales of cotton to Bimal at ₹1,500 a bale in three instalments of 40 bales. He delivers the first instalment, which Bimal accepts and uses, and then fails to deliver the rest. Bimal refuses to pay anything. Decide.

solution.provision: Quantum meruit: where a divisible contract is partly performed and the other party has accepted and enjoyed the benefit of that part, he must pay for it. Ajay remains liable in damages for his own breach.
solution.facts: The contract was divisible into instalments. Bimal accepted and used 40 bales; Ajay defaulted on the remaining instalments.
solution.analysis: Bimal cannot keep the benefit without paying for it. His remedy for the undelivered bales is a claim for damages against Ajay, which may be set off.
solution.conclusion: Bimal must pay ₹60,000 for the bales received (40 × ₹1,500); he may claim damages from Ajay for non-delivery of the rest.

checks.label: value of the first instalment accepted by the buyer

jobs.title: Customer cancels a confirmed order
jobs.situation: A customer cancels, in writing, a ₹40 lakh custom-machinery order two months before delivery. Production is 30% complete.
steps: Treat the cancellation as an anticipatory breach (Section 39).
Decide promptly: accept the repudiation and claim now, or keep the contract alive. Usually accept, to stop incurring further cost (mitigation).
Quantify: costs incurred and loss of profit arising naturally; any special loss communicated at the time of contract; the cancellation clause amount if any (Section 74 cap).
Stop further production, try to resell or reuse the work-in-progress, and document every step.
jobs.takeaway: Speed matters — every rupee spent after a clear repudiation may be a rupee you cannot recover.
jobs.think: Why should the company stop production even though it believes it will win?
jobs.answer: Because the duty to mitigate (Explanation to Section 73) means costs that could reasonably have been avoided after the breach are not recoverable.

jobs.title: Provision for liquidated damages
jobs.situation: Your client, a contractor, is 10 weeks late on a project. The contract provides ₹2 lakh per week of delay, capped at 10% of the ₹1.5 crore contract value.
steps: Compute the contractual figure: 10 weeks × ₹2 lakh = ₹20 lakh; the cap of 10% of ₹1.5 crore = ₹15 lakh.
Under Section 74 the employer can get reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum — so the maximum exposure is ₹15 lakh.
Assess with management whether a provision or a contingent-liability disclosure is appropriate, considering extensions of time and the employer's actual loss.
jobs.takeaway: Section 74 gives the ceiling; the accounting standard decides how much to provide within it.

questions.q: "An anticipatory breach of contract is a breach before the time fixed for performance." Explain, stating the rights of the aggrieved party.

model.text: Anticipatory breach occurs when, before the due date, a party refuses to perform or disables himself from performing his promise in its entirety. It may be express (a clear refusal) or implied from conduct (e.g. selling to someone else the specific goods agreed to be sold).
Section 39 lets the promisee terminate the contract, except where he has, by what he said or did, accepted that it should go on.

items: He is excused from his own performance.
Option 1: treat the contract as rescinded and sue for damages at once, without waiting for the due date.

Option 2: keep the contract alive and wait for the due date; he then holds the other party liable for non-performance — but the contract stays alive for both sides, and if a later event excuses performance, the promisor may escape liability.

model.text: Damages are assessed under Section 73 — loss arising naturally from the breach, subject to the duty to mitigate.

scheme.pt: Meaning — refusal/disablement before due date; express or implied
Option to rescind and sue immediately
Option to wait and its risk

remarks: The risk of waiting (the contract remains alive for both sides) separates good answers from average ones.
mistakes: Saying the promisee must always wait for the due date.
tips: Give one express and one implied example.

questions.q: Prakash Engineering agreed to buy 600 steel rods from Vardhan Steels at ₹950 each, delivery on 1 August, for use in a bridge project with the State Government. Prakash did not mention the Government project to Vardhan. Vardhan failed to deliver; the market price on 1 August was ₹1,080. Prakash bought rods in the market at that price, but the delay cost it a bonus of ₹2,00,000 under the Government contract. Prakash claims both the price difference and the lost bonus. Decide.

model.provision: Section 73: the injured party may recover compensation for loss that arose naturally in the usual course of things from the breach, or that both parties knew, when contracting, to be likely to result from it; not for remote or indirect loss. Hadley v. Baxendale: loss arising from special circumstances is recoverable only if those circumstances were communicated at the time of the contract.
model.facts: Contract price ₹950; market price on the due date ₹1,080; 600 rods not delivered. Prakash bought at the market price (it mitigated). Vardhan was never told of the Government contract or the bonus.
model.analysis: The price difference arises naturally from non-delivery: 600 × (₹1,080 − ₹950) = ₹78,000. The lost bonus arises from special circumstances unknown to Vardhan, so it is remote and not within the parties' contemplation.
model.conclusion: Prakash can recover ₹78,000 as ordinary damages; the claim for the lost bonus of ₹2,00,000 fails.

scheme.pt: Section 73 — natural/contemplated loss; no remote loss
Hadley v. Baxendale / need for notice of special circumstances
Bonus is special loss without notice — not recoverable

checks.label: ordinary damages for the steel rods

remarks: Many candidates award the bonus because the loss "was caused" by the breach — causation alone is not enough; foreseeability at the time of contract is required.
mistakes: Using the price Prakash finally paid instead of the market price on the due date.
Not citing Hadley v. Baxendale or the notice requirement.
tips: Separate the two heads of claim in the analysis and conclude on each.

questions.q: A lease of a warehouse provides that if the tenant vacates before 3 years he will pay the landlord ₹3,00,000 "by way of penalty". The tenant leaves after 1 year. What can the landlord recover if his loss is (a) ₹1,80,000; (b) ₹4,10,000?

model.provision: Section 74: if the contract fixes a sum payable on breach (or contains any penalty stipulation), the injured party is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named, whether the clause is called a penalty or liquidated damages.
model.facts: Named sum ₹3,00,000 "by way of penalty"; tenant broke the lease; landlord's loss (a) ₹1,80,000 or (b) ₹4,10,000.
model.analysis: The word "penalty" does not matter in India. The landlord gets reasonable compensation, but never more than the named sum.

scheme.pt: Section 74 — reasonable compensation not exceeding named sum
No distinction penalty / liquidated damages in India

checks.label: loss of ₹1,80,000 is within the named sum
loss of ₹4,10,000 — capped at the named sum

remarks: Part (b) tests whether candidates know the named sum is a ceiling.
mistakes: Holding the clause void because it says "penalty".
tips: Show both parts on separate lines in the conclusion.

questions.q: Explain the doctrine of quantum meruit and state the conditions for its application.

model.text: Quantum meruit means "as much as he has earned". Where one party has done work or supplied goods under a contract and the contract is later discharged, the law allows him reasonable payment for what he has done. The remedy is restitutory, whereas damages are compensatory.
Conditions: (1) the original contract must have been discharged; (2) the claim must be made by the party who is not in default.

items: When an agreement is discovered to be void or a contract becomes void.
When something is done without any intention of doing it gratuitously.
When services are rendered under an express or implied contract but the fee is not fixed.
When one party abandons or refuses to perform.
Where a divisible contract is partly performed and the other party enjoys the benefit.
Where a lump-sum contract is completely but badly performed — lump sum less deduction for bad work.

remarks: Both conditions must be stated to earn the middle mark.
mistakes: Allowing the party in default to claim on quantum meruit.
tips: Define in one line, then list the conditions as (1), (2).

summary: Breach: actual (on or during performance) or anticipatory (before the due date — Section 39).
Anticipatory breach: rescind and sue at once, or keep alive and wait (risk of later discharge).
Section 73: natural loss or loss contemplated by both parties; no remote/indirect loss; mitigation (Hadley v. Baxendale).
Kinds: ordinary, special, exemplary (marriage promise, cheque dishonour), nominal, deterioration by delay, pre-fixed.
Section 74: no penalty/liquidated distinction; reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum; Government bond for public duty — whole sum.
Other remedies: rescission (Section 75 compensation), quantum meruit (contract discharged, claimant not in default), specific performance, injunction.
remember: Section 39 anticipatory breach · 73 compensation · 74 named sum · 75 compensation on rightful rescission.
Damages for goods = quantity × (market price on due date − contract price).
traps: Special loss needs notice at the time of contracting — not after.
The named sum is a ceiling: never award more, may award less.
Quantum meruit is not available to the party in default.
Courts do not force personal service — they may grant an injunction on a negative promise.

viva.q: Name the kinds of damages that may be awarded for breach of contract.
viva.model: Damages may be ordinary damages for natural loss, special damages where special circumstances were made known, exemplary or vindictive damages for breach of promise to marry or wrongful dishonour of a cheque, nominal damages where no real loss is suffered, damages for deterioration caused by delay, and pre-fixed or liquidated damages.

viva.q: Distinguish specific performance from injunction as remedies for breach.
viva.model: Specific performance is an order of the court directing the party in breach to actually perform the contract, given where damages are not an adequate remedy. An injunction is an order of the court restraining a party from doing what he promised not to do.

cases.title: Spice exporter's failed shipment
cases.case: Malabar Spices agreed to buy 1,000 kg of cardamom from Kerala Growers at ₹60 per kg for delivery on 1 March, to fulfil an export order. Malabar told Kerala Growers about the export order but not that the buyer would pay a special premium. On 10 February Kerala Growers wrote that it would not deliver. Malabar accepted the refusal the same day and, on 1 March, the market price was ₹78 per kg. The contract also said Kerala Growers would pay ₹50,000 "as penalty" for any default; Malabar's total proved loss (price difference plus lost premium) is ₹70,000.

mcqs.q: The letter of 10 February is:
mcqs.explain: Refusal before the due date.

mcqs.q: Ordinary damages measured on the price difference are:
mcqs.explain: Quantity × (market price on the due date − contract price) = 1,000 × (78 − 60).

mcqs.q: The lost special premium is:
options: Not recoverable as ordinary loss — the special circumstance was not communicated
mcqs.explain: Hadley v. Baxendale — special loss needs notice at the time of contracting.

mcqs.q: Under Section 74, the upper limit (ceiling) on the compensation Malabar can be awarded under the clause is:
mcqs.explain: Reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum: the ceiling is ₹50,000 (the court fixes a reasonable amount within it and may award less). The word "penalty" does not make the clause void, and a loss above the named sum cannot lift the ceiling.
